topic: Frontier Lab · Phase 1: Compilers & Hardware Math

questions.title: JAX purity and explicit PRNG keys
questions.prompt: JAX requires pure functions and explicit random keys instead of a global RNG state. Explain why, and what breaks if you write an impure function and jit it.
probes: What specifically does jit do with your Python function that requires purity?
Why does JAX split PRNG keys instead of just calling next() on a global generator?
criteria: pure function definition
trace-then-compile mechanism
side effects only run at trace time
explicit key threading
key splitting for independence

no_hire.answer: JAX functions need to be pure because that's just how JAX works. Random keys are passed in so randomness is controlled.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No mechanism at all. Doesn't explain tracing or why purity is required, doesn't explain what splitting does.

weak_hire.answer: A pure function's output only depends on its inputs, with no side effects like mutating global state or printing. JAX traces your function once to build a computation graph and reuses it, so any side effect only happens during that first trace, not on later calls. Keys are explicit because JAX has no global mutable RNG state, so you pass a key in and get a new key out if you need more randomness.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct definition and the trace-once consequence, and knows keys are explicit, but never explains why purity is what lets jit/grad/vmap compose, and doesn't mention key splitting for independence.

hire.answer: jit traces your function with abstract tracers to build an XLA computation graph, then caches and replays that graph; if the function has side effects (print, appending to a list, reading global state) those effects fire only during the trace, so cached calls silently skip them. Purity is what makes transformations composable: grad needs a mathematically well-defined function to differentiate, vmap needs to batch the same computation over an axis, and jit needs to know the output is fully determined by the traced inputs. If randomness came from hidden global state, vmap-ing over a batch or re-running a jitted function would give inconsistent or non-reproducible results because the state mutation isn't visible to the trace. That's why PRNG keys are explicit arrays threaded through the program: you split a key into new independent keys with jax.random.split, consume one, and pass the rest onward, so randomness is a pure function of the key input.
hire.interviewer_note: Explains tracing and its interaction with side effects, connects purity to composability of jit/grad/vmap, and describes explicit key threading with split. Missing: independence guarantee of split keys and stateless functional idiom benefits at scale.

strong_hire.answer: jit lowers your Python function to a jaxpr (an IR) by running it once with abstract tracers standing in for concrete values, then compiles that jaxpr to XLA HLO and caches the compiled executable keyed on input shapes/dtypes; subsequent calls skip Python and replay the compiled graph. Purity is the precondition for every transformation: grad differentiates the jaxpr symbolically, so the function must represent a deterministic math expression, not a stateful process; vmap needs to lift the same jaxpr over a batch dimension, which only works if there's no hidden state that differs per call; and composing jit(grad(vmap(f))) requires all three to agree on what 'the function' means, which breaks the moment side effects are involved because tracing only captures the operations, not print statements, Python-level mutation, or reads of ambient global state. Impure code silently misbehaves rather than erroring: a print only fires on the trace (first call, or on retrace after a shape/dtype change), and a function that reads a global counter gives stale results because the counter's value is baked into the trace as a constant. On PRNG: since there's no global mutable generator, JAX represents random state as an explicit key array (a counter-based generator, e.g. Threefry), and jax.random.split(key, n) deterministically derives n new keys that are statistically independent of each other and of the parent, so you can fan out randomness across a program (or across vmap-ed batch elements, or pmap-ed devices) reproducibly and in parallel without any shared mutable state or sequential dependency. This also makes JAX programs trivially reproducible and parallelizable: the same key always gives the same random numbers regardless of when or how many times you call the function, which a global-state RNG cannot guarantee under jit caching, vmap batching, or multi-device execution.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Full trace-to-jaxpr-to-XLA mechanism, precise account of why purity is required for composability across jit/grad/vmap, correct diagnosis of silent impure-code failure modes (trace-time-only side effects, stale global reads), and the counter-based key/split independence argument tied to parallel and reproducible execution. Staff-level.

questions.title: jit tracing, XLA compilation, and recompilation triggers
questions.prompt: Walk me through what jit actually does to your function under the hood, and explain exactly what triggers a recompilation. Why does this make static shapes so important?
probes: Why does branching on a traced value (if x > 0) fail under jit but branching on a Python-level constant doesn't?
If you call a jitted function with the same array shape but a different value, does it recompile? Why or why not?
criteria: trace to jaxpr then XLA HLO compile
cache keyed on shapes/dtypes/static args
recompiles on shape/dtype/static-arg change, not on value change
python control flow on traced values fails
dynamic shapes cause recompilation storms / padding as fix

no_hire.answer: jit compiles your function to make it faster. It recompiles when the code changes.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No understanding of tracing, caching keys, or what actually triggers recompilation.

weak_hire.answer: jit traces your function with placeholder values to build a graph, compiles it with XLA, and caches the compiled version. If you call it again with a different input shape, it has to recompile because the graph was built for a specific shape. Regular values don't trigger recompilation, just shapes and types.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Gets the trace-compile-cache flow and that shape changes trigger recompilation, but no explanation of static args, no mention of the Python control-flow failure mode, and doesn't say why static shapes matter practically.

hire.answer: jit runs your function once with abstract tracers (which carry shape and dtype but no concrete value) to produce a jaxpr, XLA compiles that jaxpr into an executable, and the executable is cached under a key built from input shapes, dtypes, and any arguments marked static. On a later call, if the key matches, JAX replays the cached executable directly, skipping Python and retracing entirely; concrete values flowing through do not affect the key, so calling with the same shape but different numbers reuses the cache. Recompilation is triggered by: a new/changed shape, a new dtype, a different value for a static argument, or hitting a Python control-flow branch that depends on a traced value, since tracers don't have concrete values, so `if traced_value > 0` cannot be resolved at trace time and raises an error (use jax.lax.cond/select instead). Because recompilation is expensive, you want shapes to be static across calls, e.g. pad variable-length sequences to a fixed bucket size, instead of calling with a new shape every batch, which would force XLA to recompile the whole graph on every step.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct trace-to-cache-key mechanism, names shape/dtype/static-arg as the trigger, explains the traced-value control-flow failure and the lax.cond alternative, and connects to the padding-for-static-shapes practice. Missing: quantifying the compile-time cost and multi-bucket padding tradeoffs.

strong_hire.answer: jit abstractly evaluates your Python function once using tracers that encode shape and dtype (an avals abstraction, no concrete data), producing a jaxpr; that jaxpr is lowered to XLA HLO and handed to the XLA compiler, which performs fusion, layout assignment, and device-specific codegen, producing a cached executable. The cache key is (function identity, argument shapes, argument dtypes, values of any argument marked static via static_argnums/static_argnames, and pytree structure of the inputs); concrete non-static values never enter the key, so calling with a different scalar or array content but identical shape/dtype/pytree/static-args reuses the compiled executable with zero retracing cost. Recompilation happens exactly when that key changes: new shape (including batch size), new dtype, a different static arg value, or a different pytree structure (e.g. a dict with a new key). Python-level control flow (if/while/for) executes at trace time over tracers, so branching on a traced value's runtime content is impossible - the tracer has no concrete boolean to branch on - and you must use jax.lax.cond, lax.select, or lax.while_loop, which get embedded as ops in the jaxpr and executed on-device without retracing; branching on a static argument or Python int is fine because that's resolved before tracing. The reason static shapes matter operationally: XLA compilation is not cheap (can be seconds to minutes for large graphs), and shape-dependent workloads like variable-length sequences, if fed raw variable lengths, trigger a distinct compilation per unique length, a 'recompilation storm' that can dominate wall-clock time and blow out compile caches; the standard fix is bucketing/padding sequences to a small set of fixed lengths (or padding to the max and masking) so the shape space stays small and bounded, trading some wasted compute on padding tokens for avoiding per-step recompilation. In production training loops, I'd also watch for accidental shape polymorphism from Python-side logic (e.g. list comprehensions producing variable-length pytrees) since that silently reintroduces the recompilation problem jit is meant to eliminate.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Precise cache-key definition including pytree structure, exact mechanism for why traced-value branching fails at the tracer/aval level, the lax.cond/while_loop production alternative, and quantifies the real cost of recompilation storms with the bucketing/padding mitigation and its compute-waste tradeoff. Staff-level.

questions.title: Roofline model and arithmetic intensity
questions.prompt: Explain the roofline model: what is arithmetic intensity, what does compute-bound vs memory-bound mean, and where does the ridge point come from?
probes: Write the formula for arithmetic intensity and explain each term.
If a kernel's arithmetic intensity is below the ridge point, does buying a GPU with more FLOPs help? Why or why not?
criteria: arithmetic intensity = FLOPs / bytes moved
roofline = min(peak FLOPs, bandwidth * AI)
ridge point = peak FLOPs / peak bandwidth
compute-bound above ridge, memory-bound below
memory-bound kernels don't benefit from more FLOPs

no_hire.answer: Compute-bound means the GPU is doing a lot of math, and memory-bound means it's moving a lot of data. You want to be compute-bound because that's faster.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No formula, no ridge point, and the claim that compute-bound is inherently 'faster' shows no real understanding of the model.

weak_hire.answer: Arithmetic intensity is how many FLOPs you do per byte of data moved. If it's high, you're compute-bound and limited by the GPU's peak FLOPs; if it's low, you're memory-bound and limited by memory bandwidth. The roofline plot shows achievable performance as a function of arithmetic intensity.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct qualitative picture and the FLOPs-per-byte definition, but no formula for the roofline curve itself, no ridge point derivation, and doesn't answer whether more FLOPs help a memory-bound kernel.

hire.answer: Arithmetic intensity (AI) = total FLOPs performed / total bytes moved from memory. The roofline model bounds achievable performance as Performance = min(Peak FLOPs/s, Peak Bandwidth * AI): at low AI you're on the sloped line (memory-bound, more bandwidth or lower AI both hurt/help linearly), at high AI you're on the flat line (compute-bound, capped by peak FLOPs regardless of AI). The ridge point is where the two lines cross: AI_ridge = Peak FLOPs/s / Peak Bandwidth, i.e. the intensity at which you exactly saturate both compute and memory simultaneously. Below the ridge point, buying a GPU with more peak FLOPs does nothing for that kernel since it's bandwidth-limited; you'd need more bandwidth or a higher-intensity algorithm (e.g. fusing ops, larger batch/tile sizes) to move the operating point right.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct AI formula, correct roofline min() formula, correctly derives the ridge point as the FLOPs/bandwidth ratio, and correctly answers the memory-bound question with a mitigation direction. Missing: concrete numeric example and connection to real kernels like GEMM vs elementwise ops.

strong_hire.answer: Arithmetic intensity AI = FLOPs / bytes = (total floating point operations in the kernel) / (total bytes read+written from/to HBM, not registers or SRAM). The roofline bound is Perf(AI) = min(P_peak, B_peak * AI) where P_peak is the hardware's peak compute throughput (FLOPs/s) and B_peak is peak memory bandwidth (bytes/s); plotted in log-log space this is a line of slope 1 (Perf = B_peak * AI) that saturates into a flat ceiling at P_peak. The ridge point AI* = P_peak / B_peak is where the sloped and flat lines intersect - it's a hardware property, not a kernel property, and represents the FLOPs/byte ratio the hardware is 'balanced' at. Modern GPUs have very high AI* (e.g. hundreds of FLOPs/byte on an A100/H100 with tensor cores), which means most operations are memory-bound in practice: elementwise ops (activations, layernorm, dropout, softmax without fusion) have AI close to O(1) since they read and write roughly one element per FLOP, landing far left on the sloped region; dense matmul/attention with large enough tile sizes have AI that grows with matrix dimension, landing near or on the compute-bound plateau, which is why GEMM-heavy transformer layers can approach peak FLOPs while a chain of unfused pointwise ops cannot. If a kernel's operating AI is below AI*, its performance is capped at B_peak * AI regardless of P_peak, so a hardware upgrade with more FLOPs but the same bandwidth gives zero speedup - the fix is to raise AI algorithmically: kernel fusion (combine multiple pointwise ops into one pass to avoid repeated HBM round-trips, e.g. FlashAttention avoiding materializing the full attention matrix), increasing tile/block size and reuse in tiled matmul to read each byte more times relative to how much you write, or increasing batch size to amortize weight reads (exactly why LLM decode throughput scales by batching rather than by raw FLOPs). This is also why decode-phase LLM inference (low AI per step, since you touch all weights and KV cache for one token) is memory-bound while prefill (parallel over many tokens, so weight reads are amortized, higher effective AI) is compute-bound.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Precise dual formula with hardware-vs-kernel distinction, correctly derives ridge point as a hardware balance ratio, gives concrete kernel examples (elementwise vs GEMM) with AI reasoning, and connects the fusion/batching mitigations directly to real systems consequences (FlashAttention, LLM decode vs prefill). Staff-level.

questions.title: Sharding collectives: AllGather, ReduceScatter, AllReduce
questions.prompt: Explain what AllGather and ReduceScatter each do to sharded data across devices, and prove that AllReduce is equivalent to ReduceScatter followed by AllGather.
probes: What is the communication volume of each collective in terms of tensor size N and device count P?
Why do frameworks implement AllReduce as ReduceScatter+AllGather instead of a naive all-to-all sum?
criteria: AllGather: each device ends with full concatenated tensor
ReduceScatter: each device ends with its shard of the reduced sum
AllReduce = ReduceScatter then AllGather decomposition
communication volume O(N) per device with ring algorithms
why decomposition is used in practice (ZeRO/FSDP)

no_hire.answer: AllGather collects data from all devices, ReduceScatter reduces it, and AllReduce combines both of those operations somehow.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Vague restatement of names with no precise definition of inputs/outputs per device, and no actual proof or mechanism for the AllReduce decomposition.

weak_hire.answer: AllGather takes a tensor that's sharded (split) across devices and gives every device the full, concatenated tensor. ReduceScatter takes full tensors on every device, sums them elementwise, and gives each device only its shard of the result. AllReduce sums full tensors across devices and gives everyone the full sum, and you can build it by first doing a ReduceScatter to sum and shard, then an AllGather to reassemble the full sum everywhere.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct definitions of what each collective produces and states the composition correctly, but no communication volume analysis and no explanation of why this decomposition is preferred over a naive approach.

hire.answer: Given P devices each holding a shard of size N/P (or a full tensor of size N for reduction ops): AllGather takes each device's shard of size N/P and produces the full N-sized tensor on every device by concatenating shards. ReduceScatter takes a full N-sized tensor on every device (possibly different values), sums them elementwise across devices, and leaves each device with only its N/P shard of that sum. AllReduce produces the full elementwise sum of size N on every device, and it decomposes as ReduceScatter (sum and shard, giving each device its N/P piece of the total sum) followed by AllGather (reassemble those shards into the full sum everywhere) - concatenating the P shards after ReduceScatter recovers exactly the full AllReduce output since each shard is already the correctly-summed piece. Communication volume for a ring-based implementation of each collective is O(N) bytes moved per device (not O(N*P)), so AllReduce implemented this way costs about the same as two ring passes, roughly 2N bytes/device, which is why frameworks like PyTorch/NCCL use this decomposition rather than a naive all-to-all sum that would need every device to send its full tensor to every other device.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct per-device input/output shapes for all three collectives, correct proof sketch of the decomposition via shard concatenation, and states the O(N) communication volume with the practical motivation. Missing: explicit ring algorithm bandwidth formula and its role in ZeRO/FSDP specifically.

strong_hire.answer: Formally, with P devices and a tensor of logical size N: AllGather input is P shards each of size N/P (device i holds shard i), output is the full N-element tensor replicated identically on all P devices. ReduceScatter input is P full N-element tensors (one per device, values may differ, e.g. per-device gradients), output is P shards each of size N/P where shard i on device i equals shard i of the elementwise sum sum_j(tensor_j). AllReduce input is P full N-element tensors, output is the elementwise sum replicated on all P devices. Proof of AllReduce = ReduceScatter -> AllGather: after ReduceScatter, device i holds shard_i(sum_j tensor_j), i.e. exactly the i-th N/P slice of the full sum; running AllGather on these P shards concatenates shard_0, shard_1, ..., shard_{P-1} in order, which by definition reconstructs the full sum tensor, identically on every device since AllGather replicates the concatenation everywhere - this is exactly the definition of AllReduce's output, so the composition is correct by construction, not just numerically coincidental. Communication cost: with the standard ring algorithm, both AllGather and ReduceScatter move a total of (P-1)/P * N bytes per device (≈N bytes per device for large P), so composed AllReduce costs ≈2N bytes/device transferred, versus a naive all-to-all-then-reduce that would require each device to send its full N-element tensor to P-1 peers, i.e. O(N*P) traffic per device - the ring decomposition is bandwidth-optimal (achieves the theoretical lower bound of 2*(P-1)/P*N ≈ 2N) while naive all-to-all is not, which is exactly why NCCL's ring-allreduce and its ReduceScatter/AllGather building blocks are the default. This decomposition is also structurally why ZeRO-3/FSDP sharding works: instead of doing a full AllReduce on gradients (which requires materializing the full N-sized gradient on every device even though each device only needs its own optimizer-state shard), ZeRO-3 does ReduceScatter alone on the backward pass, since each device only needs its shard of the reduced gradient to update its shard of the optimizer state - skipping the AllGather half entirely saves exactly the second N bytes/device of communication and the memory to hold the full gradient, which is the core communication-memory tradeoff that makes FSDP viable at scale. Conversely FSDP's forward/backward pass needs AllGather alone (no reduction) to reconstruct full unsharded weights transiently from parameter shards before compute, then discards them - so a full FSDP training step interleaves AllGather (params, forward) and AllGather (params, backward) plus ReduceScatter (grads, backward), never a full AllReduce, which is the precise reason FSDP's communication volume per step is comparable to plain data-parallel AllReduce (≈2N total) despite sharding both parameters and gradients.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Rigorous shard-indexed proof that concatenation after ReduceScatter reconstructs AllReduce's output by construction, correct ring-algorithm bandwidth-optimality argument (≈2N vs O(NP) naive), and a precise structural connection to why ZeRO-3/FSDP uses ReduceScatter-only for grads and AllGather-only for params rather than a full AllReduce. Principal-level.

questions.title: DP vs FSDP vs TP vs PP and the pipeline bubble
questions.prompt: Compare data parallelism, FSDP/ZeRO-3, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism: what does each shard, what communication does each require, and derive the pipeline bubble fraction.
probes: Why does tensor parallelism need communication inside every layer's forward pass, while data parallelism only communicates once per step?
If you have 4 pipeline stages and only 4 microbatches, what's the bubble fraction, and why is that bad?
criteria: DP: replicates model, shards data, AllReduce grads
FSDP/ZeRO-3: shards params+grads+optimizer state, AllGather+ReduceScatter
TP: shards individual layers/matmuls, communicates per-layer
PP: shards layers across stages, bubble from fill/drain
bubble fraction = (stages-1)/(microbatches+stages-1)

no_hire.answer: DP splits the data, TP splits the model, PP splits it into stages, and FSDP is a memory-efficient version of DP. More parallelism is always better if you have more GPUs.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Surface-level labels only, no communication pattern for any of them, no bubble concept or formula, and the closing claim shows no understanding of the tradeoffs.

weak_hire.answer: DP replicates the full model on every device and splits the batch, syncing gradients with AllReduce each step. FSDP shards the model parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across devices to save memory, gathering parameters when needed for compute. TP splits individual weight matrices across devices so each device does part of every layer's computation, needing communication inside the layer. PP splits the layers of the model across devices, with each device holding some layers and passing activations to the next; this creates idle time called a bubble while the pipeline fills and drains.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct high-level characterization of what each strategy shards and roughly why each communicates, and names the bubble concept, but gives no bubble formula, no communication volume comparison, and no criteria for when to combine them.

hire.answer: DP: full model replica per device, batch sharded across devices, communication is one AllReduce of gradients per step (volume ~2x model size per device with ring algorithm), memory cost is full model+optimizer state per device which doesn't scale with device count. FSDP/ZeRO-3: parameters, gradients, and optimizer state are all sharded across devices; forward and backward each AllGather the needed layer's full parameters just-in-time then discard them, and backward does ReduceScatter instead of AllReduce on gradients since each device only needs its own shard - this trades DP's fixed per-device memory for roughly the same total communication volume, unlocking training models larger than any single device's memory. TP: individual weight matrices (e.g. attention/MLP projections) are split across devices, so every forward and backward pass through that layer requires a communication op (typically AllReduce or AllGather) to combine partial results before the next layer, meaning TP communicates far more frequently (every layer) than DP or FSDP, so it needs high-bandwidth interconnect (NVLink) and is usually kept within a node. PP: different layers live on different devices/stages, and a microbatch flows through them sequentially; the pipeline bubble is the idle time while stage 1 waits for stage 0 to produce activations at the start, and while earlier stages wait for gradients to flow back at the end. With S stages and M microbatches, bubble fraction = (S-1)/(M+S-1): more microbatches dilute the fixed fill/drain overhead, so PP needs many microbatches per batch to be efficient.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct memory/communication tradeoff for all four strategies with the right relative communication frequency ordering (TP most frequent, DP least), and states the correct bubble fraction formula. Missing: a worked numeric example and discussion of how these are combined (3D parallelism) in practice.

strong_hire.answer: Sharding axis and communication for each: DP replicates all parameters/optimizer state on every device and shards the batch; the only communication is one AllReduce of gradients per step, costing ≈2x-model-size bytes/device via ring-AllReduce, and DP's fundamental limit is memory - every device needs room for the full model, gradients, and (for Adam) ~2x params more of optimizer state, so DP alone can't train models that don't fit on one device. FSDP/ZeRO-3 shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer state into P pieces; forward does an AllGather of each layer's full parameters just before using them then frees them, backward does the same AllGather for recompute plus a ReduceScatter (not AllReduce) on gradients since each device only ever needs its own shard for its optimizer-state update - total communication volume per step is ≈3x model size (two AllGathers, one ReduceScatter, each ≈N) versus DP's ≈2x, so FSDP trades roughly 1.5x more communication for a 1/P reduction in per-device memory, which is why it's the default for models that don't fit under DP. TP shards individual matmuls (e.g. splitting the hidden dimension of an MLP or attention heads) across devices in a way where each device computes a partial result that must be combined (AllReduce) or concatenated (AllGather) before the next op can proceed correctly - this happens inside every transformer layer's forward and backward, so TP has by far the highest communication frequency and lowest tolerance for interconnect latency/bandwidth, which is why TP is almost always restricted to devices connected by NVLink within a single node, unlike DP/PP which tolerate slower cross-node links. PP assigns contiguous groups of layers to stages; a training step splits the batch into M microbatches that flow through the S stages in a pipelined fashion (GPipe-style). The bubble arises because stage s cannot start microbatch m's forward until stage s-1 finishes it, so at the start, stages 1..S-1 are idle waiting for stage 0 to produce the first microbatch's output (fill), and symmetrically at the end during the backward pass drain. Total time for one step is (M+S-1) time-steps of stage-work, of which (S-1) time-steps are pure bubble (no useful stage is doing real work relative to the ideal M steps of full pipeline utilization), giving bubble fraction = (S-1)/(M+S-1); as M grows relative to S, the fraction shrinks toward 0, which is why PP requires many microbatches (often the global batch split finely) to be efficient, and why more pipeline stages need proportionally more microbatches to keep the bubble small. In production, frontier training combines all of these as 3D (or 4D with sequence/context parallelism) parallelism: TP within a node (few devices, high communication tolerance from NVLink), PP across node groups (coarse-grained, communication only at stage boundaries, tolerant of the bubble if microbatch count is high), and DP/FSDP across the outermost replica groups (least frequent communication, tolerates cross-datacenter-ish links); the choice of degree along each axis is itself an optimization problem trading memory, bubble fraction, and communication volume against the actual interconnect topology.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Precise communication-volume accounting for all four strategies including the exact ≈2x vs ≈3x model-size comparison between DP and FSDP, correct explanation of why TP's frequency forces it onto NVLink while PP/DP tolerate slower links, rigorous derivation of the bubble fraction from fill+drain timesteps, and ties everything together into the real 3D/4D parallelism topology-aware design used at frontier scale. Staff-level.

questions.title: Training memory footprint and activation checkpointing
questions.prompt: A model fits comfortably in memory for inference but OOMs during training with the exact same batch size. Break down where all the training memory goes, and explain how activation checkpointing fixes this and what it costs.
probes: Why does Adam specifically roughly double the memory cost of just storing the gradients?
If you checkpoint every layer, what's the recompute cost, and is there a better strategy than checkpointing everything or nothing?
criteria: inference needs only weights + KV/activations for current step
training adds gradients (1x params) and optimizer state (~2x params for Adam)
activation memory scales with batch size, sequence length, and number of layers, absent at inference in that form
checkpointing trades stored activations for recomputation in backward pass
sqrt(L) checkpointing strategy / selective checkpointing tradeoff

no_hire.answer: Training uses more memory because you need gradients too, and gradients take a lot of space. You can fix OOM by using a smaller batch size.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Names gradients but no accounting of optimizer state or activations, no mechanism for why activations specifically blow up, and no mention of activation checkpointing at all despite being asked directly.

weak_hire.answer: Inference only needs the model weights and some activations for the current forward pass. Training also needs to store gradients for every parameter and the optimizer's state (like Adam's momentum and variance terms), plus it has to keep all the intermediate activations from the forward pass around so it can compute gradients in the backward pass, which is why memory blows up even at the same batch size. Activation checkpointing saves memory by not storing all activations and recomputing some of them during the backward pass instead.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct qualitative list of what training adds and correctly identifies why activations must be retained for backward, and states checkpointing's basic trade, but gives no numeric accounting (e.g. the ~2x for Adam) and no cost/benefit analysis of checkpointing strategy.

hire.answer: Inference memory is roughly just the weights (N params * bytes/param) plus a small amount for the current activations/KV cache, which don't grow with anything you store long-term. Training memory adds: gradients, one value per parameter, so +1x params in the same dtype; and for Adam, optimizer state stores the first and second moment (momentum and variance) per parameter, so +2x params (often kept in FP32 even under mixed precision, making this the single biggest addition); and critically, activation memory - during the forward pass you must retain every intermediate activation needed to compute gradients in the backward pass, and this scales with batch size * sequence length * number of layers * hidden size, which at training batch sizes and with backprop's memory requirement (versus inference which discards each layer's activation immediately after using it) is often the dominant term, not the parameters. This is exactly why the same batch size that fits at inference OOMs at training - inference discards activations layer by layer, training must hold onto all of them until the backward pass consumes them. Activation checkpointing (gradient checkpointing) fixes this by not storing every layer's activations; instead it stores only a subset (e.g. every k-th layer) and recomputes the missing ones by rerunning the forward pass for that segment during backward, trading roughly 30-40% extra compute (an extra forward pass through the checkpointed segments) for a significant reduction in peak activation memory, often enough to unblock training that would otherwise OOM.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct full memory breakdown with the right relative magnitudes (Adam's 2x, activations scaling with batch*seq*layers), correctly explains the inference-vs-training discard difference, and correctly describes checkpointing's recompute-for-memory trade with a reasonable compute overhead estimate. Missing: the sqrt(L) optimal checkpointing strategy and selective/partial checkpointing nuance.

strong_hire.answer: Precise accounting for a model with P parameters in training with Adam and mixed precision: (1) weights, ~2P bytes in FP16/BF16 for compute plus often a master copy in FP32 (4P bytes) for stable updates; (2) gradients, ~2P bytes matching the compute dtype; (3) Adam optimizer state, first moment (momentum) and second moment (variance), each typically kept in FP32 for numerical stability, so 4P + 4P = 8P bytes - this is why 'Adam roughly doubles' isn't quite right in absolute terms, it's actually the single largest fixed cost, often exceeding the weights+gradients combined, which is precisely why memory-efficient optimizers (8-bit Adam, Adafactor) or optimizer state sharding (ZeRO-1) target this term first; (4) activations, which unlike the fixed P-scaling terms above, scale as O(batch * seq_len * hidden_dim * num_layers * (some constant factor from attention/MLP intermediate tensors, e.g. ~roughly 12-20x hidden_dim per layer for a standard transformer block including attention scores, softmax outputs, and MLP intermediate activations)) - this term has no analogue at the same magnitude during inference because inference is either single-token decode (activations are O(1) per step, dominated by the KV cache instead) or a one-shot prefill that discards each layer's activations immediately after use, while training's backward pass requires the entire forward computation graph's intermediates to remain resident simultaneously until consumed by backprop. This is the exact mechanism behind 'fits at inference, OOMs at training with the same batch size': inference never needs all L layers' activations alive at once, training does. Activation checkpointing addresses the activation term specifically (it does nothing for weights/gradients/optimizer state) by discarding intermediate activations after the forward pass and recomputing them on-demand during backward: naive full checkpointing (checkpoint every layer) reduces activation memory from O(L) to O(1) per checkpointed segment but costs a full extra forward pass, roughly +33% compute (one extra forward relative to one forward + one backward, since backward is roughly 2x the forward FLOPs). The provably-optimal strategy, when you can choose which layers to checkpoint, is to checkpoint every sqrt(L)-th layer: this achieves O(sqrt(L)) activation memory (versus O(L) uncheckpointed or O(1) for full checkpointing, which recomputes the most) with an asymptotically favorable memory/recompute tradeoff, a result from Chen et al.'s gradient checkpointing analysis, and it strictly dominates the two naive extremes for large L. Selective/partial checkpointing goes further in practice: checkpoint only the layers with the largest activation footprint relative to recompute cost (e.g. checkpoint attention but not cheap elementwise ops, or checkpoint MLP intermediates which are large but cheap to recompute), which is what production frameworks like Megatron's selective activation checkpointing implement, since not all layers have the same memory-to-recompute-cost ratio and blanket checkpointing wastes compute on layers where the memory saved is small.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Rigorous byte-level accounting distinguishing compute-dtype vs FP32-master-copy costs, correctly identifies Adam's optimizer state as often the single largest term (not merely 'roughly doubles' gradients), precisely explains the inference-vs-training asymmetry via computation-graph liveness, and gives the sqrt(L) optimal checkpointing result with the selective/partial checkpointing production refinement.
